Security.title: Find which prospects run Shopify, HubSpot or Microsoft 365, from a list of domains
Security.summary:
A lot of B2B selling starts with "what do they run?". A Shopify app developer wants the stores on Shopify, an agency wants the sites with no ad pixel, an email security vendor wants the companies on Microsoft 365 without a DMARC policy. The answer is sitting in each company's homepage and DNS records; reading it for a few thousand domains by hand is the problem.

This post turns a domain list into a segmented prospect sheet in Python, then compares the tech stack lookup tools on the Apify Store using the prices their Store pages listed at the time of writing.

Disclosure: I'm Aurelix, and I built the Tech Stack API. It's a paid tool (prices below). Check each Store page before you buy: prices change.

What one row tells you

Each domain is read live: its homepage once (robots.txt obeyed) and its public MX, SPF, DMARC and NS records. One row per domain:

  • One column per category, as a list of names: cms, ecommerce, analytics, tag_manager, advertising (Meta Pixel, Google Ads, LinkedIn, TikTok...), chat, crm_marketing, payments, consent, framework, backend, web_server, cdn_hosting.
  • Email from DNS: email_provider (Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, Zoho...), email_security (a gateway such as Mimecast or Proofpoint), email_sender (sending services named in SPF), dmarc_policy (none, quarantine or reject), plus the raw mx and spf.
  • dns_provider, technologies (every detection as name and category), homepage_checked, and a note when the homepage could not be read.

When a site blocks bots, the row still carries the DNS fields, which is often enough to segment by email provider.

From a domain list to segments 

pip install apify-client

import csv
import os
from collections import Counter

from apify_client import ApifyClient

DOMAINS = ["allbirds.com", "davidstea.com", "webflow.com", "hubspot.com", "mcgill.ca", "wordpress.org"]

client = ApifyClient(os.environ["APIFY_TOKEN"])
run = client.actor("aurelix/tech-stack-detector").call(run_input={"domains": DOMAINS})
rows = list(client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items())

cols = ["domain", "cms", "ecommerce", "analytics", "advertising", "chat", "crm_marketing",
        "email_provider", "email_security", "dmarc_policy", "homepage_checked", "note"]
with open("stacks.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    w = csv.writer(f)
    w.writerow(cols)
    for r in rows:
        w.writerow(["; ".join(r[c]) if isinstance(r[c], list) else r[c] for c in cols])

shopify = [r["domain"] for r in rows if "Shopify" in r["ecommerce"]]
no_pixel = [r["domain"] for r in rows if r["homepage_checked"] and not r["advertising"]]
weak_dmarc = [r["domain"] for r in rows if r["email_provider"] and r["dmarc_policy"] in (None, "none")]
print("On Shopify:", shopify)
print("No ad pixel on the homepage:", no_pixel)
print("Email provider found, DMARC missing or monitor-only:", weak_dmarc)
print("Email providers:", Counter(r["email_provider"] or "unknown" for r in rows).most_common())

Each segment is a different conversation: Shopify stores for an app or agency, sites with no ad pixel for a paid-ads pitch, a missing or monitor-only DMARC policy for an email security vendor. homepage_checked matters for the second one: an empty advertising list only means "none found" when the homepage was actually read.

Where the domains come from:

  • Your CRM or a purchased list: paste the domains or full URLs; only the host is used, so https://apify.com/store and APIFY.COM count as one domain.
  • A local business list: run the Google Maps Phone Scraper for a category and city; its website column is this tool's domains input, and cms then shows who is on Wix, Squarespace or WordPress.

Tech stack lookup tools on the Apify Store compared

Prices per 1,000 domains from each Store page at the time of writing:

Free plan $1.50 $2.00 $0.24 $10.00 per site with a detection
Bronze $1.05 $2.00 $0.21 $10.00
Gold $1.05 $2.00 $0.13 $10.00
Start fee per run $0.001 none $0.005 none
Where the data comes from live homepage + DNS BuiltWith's own database live pages, 1 to 5 per domain live site
Email provider (MX), SPF senders, DMARC policy yes not stated not stated not stated
One column per category yes not stated flat list of categories not stated
Confidence and evidence per detection no not stated yes not stated
Unreachable domains free yes not stated not stated yes

Where each wins: automation-lab is far cheaper per domain than any of the others, can read several pages per domain, and gives a confidence score and the evidence behind each match; for bulk enrichment of technology names alone, it's the one to try first. BuiltWith's official tool is the most used and draws on BuiltWith's own database rather than a single live visit. scrapemint charges only for sites where it found something. The Aurelix tool fits when the email side matters as much as the website: mailbox provider, security gateway, SPF senders and DMARC policy from DNS on every row, in flat CRM-ready columns, still filled in when the homepage blocks bots.

Limits

  • Homepage only, no JavaScript. Tools loaded later by a tag manager, only on inner pages, or only after cookie consent can be missed. Tag managers themselves are detected.
  • No history. No first-seen dates or spend estimates; each run is a fresh read, and there is no change-only mode.
  • Rule-based detection from our own fingerprint rules (not Wappalyzer or BuiltWith data); a rare false match or miss is possible, and versions are not reported.
  • SPF is read one level deep: includes are matched by name, nested includes and redirects are not followed.
  • Blocked sites get the DNS fields only, with homepage_checked false and a note saying why.
  • Speed: ten domains at a time, about 40 to 60 a minute; for lists above about 2,500 domains, raise the run timeout.

Cost

You pay per domain analysed. A domain whose homepage is blocked is still charged once, because its row carries the DNS fields; domains that neither resolve nor answer, and duplicates in the input, are free. The current price per domain is on the Store page; Apify's free plan includes $5 of credit a month, enough for a few thousand domains.

Security.title: The Pragmatic 3-Step Roadmap to UBI: Start by Doubling Rural Pensions and Universal Child Allowances
Security.summary:
Whenever we discuss Universal Basic Income (UBI) in the age of AI, the most common objection in the comments is always the same:

"The philosophy sounds great, but paying 1.4 billion people even a modest monthly stipend would cost trillions! Where does the money come from? If we can't fund full universal coverage tomorrow morning, isn't UBI just a utopian daydream?"

This objection sounds hard-headed, but it commits a classic all-or-nothing engineering fallacy.

Look back at the history of modern social contracts over the past two centuries—whether universal public education in the 19th century or social security and universal healthcare in the 20th. Not a single transformative social safety net launched on Day One with 100% population coverage and 100% payout levels. Every one of them followed a staged engineering rollout: starting with the most vulnerable groups where marginal utility and social consensus were highest, proving the fiscal multiplier, and then scaling to universal coverage as industrial productivity surged.

As AI agents and humanoid robots rapidly automate cognitive and physical labor in 2026, abundant productivity must translate into human freedom and dignity, not existential fear. We do not need to wait a decade for an overnight miracle. We can launch a crystal-clear, fiscally grounded 3-Step UBI Engineering Roadmap today.

Step 1 (Immediate Launch): Double Rural Basic Pensions and Issue Unconditional Monthly Child Allowances

Why must Phase 1 target seniors and young children first?

Because every dollar invested at the two ends of the human lifecycle delivers an immediate macroeconomic multiplier while relieving the heaviest financial pressure on working-age families—with zero ideological debate about "discouraging work." A 70-year-old rural farmer and a 3-year-old toddler should never be forced to compete in the labor market.

Let's run the exact fiscal math:

1. Raise Rural and Non-Working Basic Pensions from ~200 RMB to 800–1,000 RMB/Month

Roughly 170 million seniors in China—mostly rural parents who built the nation's agricultural and industrial foundation—currently receive a baseline pension of only 150 to 250 RMB per month.

  • Raising their unconditional baseline pension by 600 RMB per month requires an annual outlay of roughly 1.22 trillion RMB (less than 1% of national GDP), easily funded by transferring state-owned capital dividends and early AI infrastructure taxes.
  • The Multiplier Effect: Low-income seniors have a marginal propensity to consume above 0.85. Nearly every yuan flows immediately into local groceries, healthcare, and household goods, while lifting a massive financial and emotional burden off hundreds of millions of working-age children.

2. An Unconditional 800 RMB/Month Child Allowance for Every Child Aged 0–6

With roughly 75 million children under age six, issuing an automatic, means-test-free 800 RMB monthly child allowance directly to mothers costs roughly 720 billion RMB per year.

  • Combined, protecting both seniors and young children requires under 2 trillion RMB annually—a fraction of traditional infrastructure stimulus, yet infinitely more effective at reviving household consumption confidence.

Step 2 (Years 3–5): Launch the "Youth AI Transition & Creator Basic Stipend"

Once the household floor for seniors and children is secured, Phase 2 addresses the demographic hit hardest by white-collar and factory automation: working-age adults aged 22 to 45.

Traditional unemployment insurance suffers from a fatal design flaw known as the welfare cliff: the moment an unemployed worker earns a few hundred dollars driving a gig car or building an indie app, their benefits are cut off. This traps people in short-term survival anxiety instead of allowing them to reskill.

Phase 2 replaces punitive unemployment insurance with an unconditional AI Transition & Creator Stipend:

  1. No Welfare Cliff: Workers in structurally automating sectors receive a baseline 1,500–2,000 RMB monthly floor that does not vanish when they earn side income building AI products, teaching, or creating art.
  2. Universal Compute Vouchers: Alongside cash, every citizen receives a monthly quota of public frontier AI tokens and cloud compute—ensuring that the tools of AI creation belong to everyone, not just tech monopolies.

Step 3 (Years 5–10): Merge into Full Universal Compute & Automation Dividends (Full UBI)

As humanoid robots scale across manufacturing, agriculture, and construction, and AI agents handle 80% of routine cognitive workflows, the marginal cost of physical goods and digital services will plummet toward zero.

At that point, the direct digital disbursement rails and sovereign dividend pools built in Steps 1 and 2 seamlessly expand into Full Universal Basic Income:

  • Self-Sustaining Sovereign Pool: A 2% to 5% Automation & Token Dividend Tax on commercial compute clusters and autonomous robotic fleets funds the national dividend pool.
  • Survival Decoupled from Labor: Every citizen receives a lifelong monthly dividend guaranteeing housing, nutrition, healthcare, and creative freedom as a birthright.

Conclusion: A Bridge to the Stars Is Built One Brick at a Time

Never let the difficulty of Step 3 become an excuse to delay Step 1. Doubling the pensions of elderly parents and issuing unconditional child allowances today is the first concrete brick of the AI century's new social contract.

Security.title: Planning an AI short-drama pipeline without buying a new GPU
Security.summary:
Before buying more hardware for AI video, compare the cost of upgrading with renting for the stages that need a GPU. Our ep05 explainer discusses that decision (video link below); this article proposes a workflow, not a completed production benchmark.

If you would rather defer a hardware purchase, one possible setup is to run the light stages through an API and rent a GPU for the stages that need your own model weights.

Untested example: The snippets below were checked against public documentation, not executed. They are illustrative, not a tested end-to-end workflow; add error handling, timeouts and output checks before use. Catalog presence is not proof of successful inference or current GPU stock.

The pipeline, stage by stage

An episode of a vertical short drama (a minute or two, 15–30 shots) breaks down like this:

Stage What runs Where it runs well
Series bible + episode script a large chat model API
Shot list + image/video prompts a fast chat model API
Keyframes / character sheets FLUX API, or ComfyUI on a GPU if you use a character LoRA
Shots Model supporting the required input API for supported shots; custom ComfyUI workflows on a GPU sized for the workload
Voice TTS API
Subtitles Whisper API

The rule of thumb: anything stateless and prompt-driven goes to an API. Anything that needs your weights (a character LoRA, a custom ComfyUI graph) goes on a GPU you control, for as long as the render takes.

1. Script and shot list over an OpenAI-compatible API

The OpenAI Python and Node SDKs are documented for chat completions with a CloudGPU base URL and key; that does not imply every SDK feature is supported. A large model writes the episode and a fast one turns it into shots:

import os, json
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    api_key=os.environ["CLOUDGPU_API_KEY"],
    base_url="https://cloudgpu.app/v1",
)

bible = open("series_bible.md").read()   # characters, tone, recurring props

episode = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="deepseek-v4-pro",
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": "You write 90-second vertical drama episodes. Keep names and facts consistent with the bible."},
        {"role": "user", "content": bible + "\n\nWrite episode 4: the sister finds the letter."},
    ],
).choices[0].message.content

shots = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="deepseek-v4-flash",
    response_format={"type": "json_object"},
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": 'Split the script into shots. Return {"shots":[{"id":1,"seconds":4,"image_prompt":"...","motion_prompt":"...","line":"..."}]}'},
        {"role": "user", "content": episode},
    ],
).choices[0].message.content

shots = json.loads(shots)["shots"]
print(len(shots), "shots")

Keep the bible as a file in the repo and send it with every episode. It can help consistency, but review each generated script; it is not a guarantee.

2. Quick shots through the video endpoint

For establishing shots and B-roll that don't need a locked character, a video job is enough. It's asynchronous: create, poll, download.

import time, requests

H = {"Authorization": "Bearer " + os.environ["CLOUDGPU_API_KEY"]}
BASE = "https://cloudgpu.app/v1"

job = requests.post(f"{BASE}/videos", headers=H, json={
    "model": "wan-3.0",
    "prompt": shots[0]["image_prompt"] + ". " + shots[0]["motion_prompt"],
}).json()

while True:
    status = requests.get(f"{BASE}/videos/{job['id']}", headers=H).json()["status"]
    if status in ("completed", "failed"):
        break
    time.sleep(10)

if status == "completed":
    mp4 = requests.get(f"{BASE}/videos/{job['id']}/content", headers=H)
    open("shot_01.mp4", "wb").write(mp4.content)

Optional fields (resolution, seconds, and image for models that accept images) are listed in the API docs. The current catalog lists wan-3.0 as text-to-video only; use an image-capable model for image-to-video. Finished files are downloadable for 24 hours, so pull them into your own storage.

3. Character shots on a rented GPU

When the lead has to look the same in every shot, you want your own LoRA and your own ComfyUI graph. VRAM requirements depend on the workflow, precision, resolution and offloading. CloudGPU's published Wan 2.2 test reports about 21 GB peak VRAM for its tested 14B FP8 configuration; do not treat 24 GB or 48 GB as a universal requirement.

Instead of buying that card, start one only for the render batch. The GPU API documents server-enforced auto-shutdown limits. Set and monitor appropriate limits; they do not replace copying outputs before destruction:

templates = requests.get(f"{BASE}/gpu/templates", headers=H).json()
comfy = next(t for t in templates["data"] if "comfyui" in t["name"].lower())

inst = requests.post(f"{BASE}/gpu/instances", headers=H, json={
    "template": comfy["id"],
    "gpu_model": "auto",       # or pick a card from GET /gpu/offers
    "idle_minutes": 30,        # destroy after 30 idle minutes
    "max_minutes": 240,        # hard cap for this batch
}).json()
print(inst["id"], inst["status"])

Then SSH in, pull your LoRA and workflow, queue the shots, copy the MP4s out, and destroy the instance (DELETE /gpu/instances/{id}). Billing is per minute, rounded up, with a 1-minute minimum; billing stops when you destroy the instance. Check the live deploy page for which cards are available that day.

(The response shape above is simplified; check GET /v1/gpu/templates once and adjust the field names to what it returns.)

4. Voice and subtitles

Both are OpenAI-format audio endpoints, so the same client works:

speech = client.audio.speech.create(model="kokoro-tts", voice="af_heart", input=shots[0]["line"])
speech.write_to_file("line_01.mp3")

with open("episode_04_rough.mp4", "rb") as f:
    srt = client.audio.transcriptions.create(model="whisper-v3-turbo", file=f, response_format="srt")
open("episode_04.srt", "w").write(srt)

(Voice names depend on the TTS model; list them from the docs.)

Rent or buy?

We won't quote prices here because they move. Do the math with your own numbers:

  • Hours per month you actually need a big card (renders + LoRA training, not editing).
  • The card's local price today, plus the RAM and SSD you'd also upgrade.
  • How long until you'd upgrade again.

If the big-card hours are a few sessions a month, renting keeps the money in your pocket and nothing sits idle. Daily rendering can change the calculation; compare hardware, electricity, utilization and cloud costs rather than assuming buying always wins.

That's also the takeaway from ep05: buy what you need, don't hoard, and for the occasional big job, rent the kitchen instead of building one.

  • Per-stage GPU guide for short dramas: https://cloudgpu.app/cloud-gpu-for-ai-short-drama?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=article&utm_campaign=202611_seg03_freelancer_gpu_api&utm_content=devto_drama_pipeline_rent

Frontend.title: Find which prospects run Shopify, HubSpot or Microsoft 365, from a list of domains
Frontend.summary:
A lot of B2B selling starts with "what do they run?". A Shopify app developer wants the stores on Shopify, an agency wants the sites with no ad pixel, an email security vendor wants the companies on Microsoft 365 without a DMARC policy. The answer is sitting in each company's homepage and DNS records; reading it for a few thousand domains by hand is the problem.

This post turns a domain list into a segmented prospect sheet in Python, then compares the tech stack lookup tools on the Apify Store using the prices their Store pages listed at the time of writing.

Disclosure: I'm Aurelix, and I built the Tech Stack API. It's a paid tool (prices below). Check each Store page before you buy: prices change.

What one row tells you

Each domain is read live: its homepage once (robots.txt obeyed) and its public MX, SPF, DMARC and NS records. One row per domain:

  • One column per category, as a list of names: cms, ecommerce, analytics, tag_manager, advertising (Meta Pixel, Google Ads, LinkedIn, TikTok...), chat, crm_marketing, payments, consent, framework, backend, web_server, cdn_hosting.
  • Email from DNS: email_provider (Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, Zoho...), email_security (a gateway such as Mimecast or Proofpoint), email_sender (sending services named in SPF), dmarc_policy (none, quarantine or reject), plus the raw mx and spf.
  • dns_provider, technologies (every detection as name and category), homepage_checked, and a note when the homepage could not be read.

When a site blocks bots, the row still carries the DNS fields, which is often enough to segment by email provider.

From a domain list to segments 

pip install apify-client

import csv
import os
from collections import Counter

from apify_client import ApifyClient

DOMAINS = ["allbirds.com", "davidstea.com", "webflow.com", "hubspot.com", "mcgill.ca", "wordpress.org"]

client = ApifyClient(os.environ["APIFY_TOKEN"])
run = client.actor("aurelix/tech-stack-detector").call(run_input={"domains": DOMAINS})
rows = list(client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items())

cols = ["domain", "cms", "ecommerce", "analytics", "advertising", "chat", "crm_marketing",
        "email_provider", "email_security", "dmarc_policy", "homepage_checked", "note"]
with open("stacks.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    w = csv.writer(f)
    w.writerow(cols)
    for r in rows:
        w.writerow(["; ".join(r[c]) if isinstance(r[c], list) else r[c] for c in cols])

shopify = [r["domain"] for r in rows if "Shopify" in r["ecommerce"]]
no_pixel = [r["domain"] for r in rows if r["homepage_checked"] and not r["advertising"]]
weak_dmarc = [r["domain"] for r in rows if r["email_provider"] and r["dmarc_policy"] in (None, "none")]
print("On Shopify:", shopify)
print("No ad pixel on the homepage:", no_pixel)
print("Email provider found, DMARC missing or monitor-only:", weak_dmarc)
print("Email providers:", Counter(r["email_provider"] or "unknown" for r in rows).most_common())

Each segment is a different conversation: Shopify stores for an app or agency, sites with no ad pixel for a paid-ads pitch, a missing or monitor-only DMARC policy for an email security vendor. homepage_checked matters for the second one: an empty advertising list only means "none found" when the homepage was actually read.

Where the domains come from:

  • Your CRM or a purchased list: paste the domains or full URLs; only the host is used, so https://apify.com/store and APIFY.COM count as one domain.
  • A local business list: run the Google Maps Phone Scraper for a category and city; its website column is this tool's domains input, and cms then shows who is on Wix, Squarespace or WordPress.

Where each wins: automation-lab is far cheaper per domain than any of the others, can read several pages per domain, and gives a confidence score and the evidence behind each match; for bulk enrichment of technology names alone, it's the one to try first. BuiltWith's official tool is the most used and draws on BuiltWith's own database rather than a single live visit. scrapemint charges only for sites where it found something. The Aurelix tool fits when the email side matters as much as the website: mailbox provider, security gateway, SPF senders and DMARC policy from DNS on every row, in flat CRM-ready columns, still filled in when the homepage blocks bots.

Limits

  • Homepage only, no JavaScript. Tools loaded later by a tag manager, only on inner pages, or only after cookie consent can be missed. Tag managers themselves are detected.
  • No history. No first-seen dates or spend estimates; each run is a fresh read, and there is no change-only mode.
  • Rule-based detection from our own fingerprint rules (not Wappalyzer or BuiltWith data); a rare false match or miss is possible, and versions are not reported.
  • SPF is read one level deep: includes are matched by name, nested includes and redirects are not followed.
  • Blocked sites get the DNS fields only, with homepage_checked false and a note saying why.
  • Speed: ten domains at a time, about 40 to 60 a minute; for lists above about 2,500 domains, raise the run timeout.

You pay per domain analysed. Frontend.title: My Analytics Agent Stopped Repeating Its Wrong Guesses With Hindsight
Frontend.summary:
My Analytics Agent Stopped Repeating Its Wrong Guesses With Hindsight

Every Monday morning, someone in leadership asks why a regional revenue metric dropped, and an analyst spends two hours checking the exact same five tables in the exact same order. When we first wired an LLM tool-calling agent to automate root-cause investigations, it had an infuriating habit: it treated every single alert like its first day on the job.

If the South region experienced three consecutive pricing-tier drops over three weeks, a stateless agent would still burn time querying holiday calendars, competitor promo trackers, and warehouse stockout logs before checking pricing. Worse, if the Monday morning ETL sync stalled at 02:00 UTC, the agent would panic over incomplete tables and report a fake revenue collapse. And no matter how many times the Finance Head asked for a single-line summary with the exact dollar variance, the next session returned a multi-paragraph essay.

To fix this, we built WhyDesk—an autonomous metric investigation system powered by FastAPI, Groq tool-calling, and the Hindsight GitHub repository. Instead of treating memory as a passive chat log, we used Vectorize agent memory to dynamically reorder diagnostic tool execution, skip low-probability checks, flag flaky data pipelines before trusting raw numbers, and enforce stakeholder-specific output formatting.

What the System Does and How It Hangs Together

WhyDesk sits between business stakeholders (Finance Head and Senior Analyst) and five deterministic diagnostic tools that inspect weekly regional performance across South, North, West, and East:

  • check_holiday_calendar: Audits regional banking holidays and seasonal B2B checkout dips.
  • check_competitor_promos: Scans market intelligence feeds for aggressive rival discounting.
  • check_inventory_stockouts: Inspects warehouse SKU depletion and unfulfilled hardware bundle backlogs.
  • check_pricing_changes: Audits contract repricing, partner promo codes, discount overrides, and unit ACV shifts.
  • check_etl_pipeline: Verifies warehouse sync completion, job timestamps, and missing row counts.

When an investigation request arrives at POST /api/investigate, WhyDesk does not immediately hand the five tool schemas to the LLM. Instead, it executes a four-stage loop built around the primitives described in what Hindsight does:

User Query + Stakeholder Role
       │
       ▼
1. Hindsight Recall (world, experience, observation) + Reflect
       │
       ▼
2. Memory-Driven Tool Planner (Groq qwen/qwen3-32b -> openai/gpt-oss-120b -> llama-3.3-70b-versatile)
   [Reorders diagnostic tools & enables early stopping once root cause + clean ETL are verified]
       │
       ▼
3. Deterministic Tool Execution + Numeric Grounding Verification
       │
       ▼
4. Synchronous Hindsight Retain (Confirmed cause, ruled-out theories, pipeline reliability, format rule)

Core Technical Story: Turning Memory Into Tool Execution Order

Most agent implementations stuff retrieved text chunks into a prompt and hope the model changes its behavior. In data analysis, passive context is not enough. We needed institutional memory to govern which diagnostic tools run first, which tools get skipped, and how the final answer is shaped.

We organized our Hindsight memory bank (whydesk-bank) around three memory types and configured the bank disposition with high skepticism and literalism (skepticism: 4, literalism: 4, empathy: 2) so confirmed metric verdicts always outweigh unverified guesses:

  1. World facts (world): Confirmed historical root causes and explicitly falsified hypotheses for a region or product line (for example, "In W10 and W12 for the South region, revenue drops were caused by pricing configuration changes; holiday and competitor promo hypotheses were ruled out").
  2. Operational experiences (experience): Lessons learned about data source reliability (for example, "Monday revenue drops in W11 were false alarms caused by an etl_sales_sync warehouse stall; always verify ETL pipeline status before trusting Monday numbers").
  3. Stakeholder observations (observation): Reporting rules per persona (for example, "Stakeholder 'Finance Head' strictly requires a 1-line summary with the exact dollar impact").

1. Pre-Investigation Recall and Reflection (backend/memory.py)

Before calling Groq, WhyDeskMemory.recall_context() queries Hindsight across all three memory types and runs reflect() to synthesize a tactical plan for the current investigation:

def recall_context(self, question: str, region: str, stakeholder: str) -> dict:
    query = (
        f"Past metric investigations for region {region}, reliable vs unreliable data sources, "
        f"ruled out causes, and formatting preferences for stakeholder {stakeholder}. "
        f"Question: {question}"
    )
    recall_resp = self.client.recall(
        bank_id=self.bank_id,
        query=query,
        types=["world", "experience", "observation"],
        budget="mid",
        max_tokens=2048,
    )

    memories = [
        {
            "id": getattr(r, "id", ""),
            "text": getattr(r, "text", ""),
            "type": getattr(r, "type", "world"),
            "context": getattr(r, "context", ""),
        }
        for r in (recall_resp.results or [])
    ]

    reflect_resp = self.client.reflect(
        bank_id=self.bank_id,
        query=(
            f"Based on past investigations in {region} and stakeholder {stakeholder}: "
            f"1) Which diagnostic tools should run first? "
            f"2) Which hypotheses were repeatedly ruled out? "
            f"3) Any data pipeline traps to check first? "
            f"4) How should the final response for {stakeholder} be formatted?"
        ),
        budget="low",
    )

    return {
        "query": query,
        "memories": memories,
        "reflection": getattr(reflect_resp, "text", ""),
    }

2. Memory-Driven Tool Ordering and Early Stopping (backend/agent.py)

Rather than hardcoding regional rules in Python, backend/agent.py derives the diagnostic execution queue strictly from the recalled memory text and reflection output. On a cold start (0 recalled memories) or when the user switches the UI toggle to Memory off, the agent runs all five tools in the default baseline sequence (check_holiday_calendar -> check_competitor_promos -> check_inventory_stockouts -> check_pricing_changes -> check_etl_pipeline).

When Memory on is active and Hindsight returns prior investigations, the planner scores each diagnostic tool based on recalled pipeline warnings, historical regional root causes, and previously ruled-out checks:

def derive_tool_order_from_memory(memories: list[dict], reflection: str) -> list[str]:
    combined = " ".join(m.get("text", "") for m in memories) + " " + (reflection or "")
    text = combined.lower()

    if not text.strip():
        return list(DEFAULT_TOOL_ORDER)

    priority_scores = {tool: 0 for tool in DEFAULT_TOOL_ORDER}

    if "etl" in text or "pipeline" in text or "sync" in text or "lag" in text:
        priority_scores["check_etl_pipeline"] += 30
    if "pricing" in text or "discount" in text or "promo code" in text or "repricing" in text:
        priority_scores["check_pricing_changes"] += 20
    if "stockout" in text or "inventory" in text:
        priority_scores["check_inventory_stockouts"] += 15
    if "ruled out" in text and "holiday" in text:
        priority_scores["check_holiday_calendar"] -= 10
    if "ruled out" in text and "competitor" in text:
        priority_scores["check_competitor_promos"] -= 10

    return sorted(
        DEFAULT_TOOL_ORDER,
        key=lambda t: (-priority_scores[t], DEFAULT_TOOL_ORDER.index(t)),
    )

Once the prioritized tools run, the agent checks whether the warehouse ETL sync is verified clean and a primary anomaly (status == "anomaly_detected") has been isolated. When both conditions are met under memory-guided execution, the loop stops early and skips the remaining low-probability checks.

3. Synchronous Post-Investigation Retention (backend/memory.py)

In an interactive analytics workflow, an analyst often runs follow-up investigations seconds apart. If memory ingestion happens asynchronously in the background, the very next query might miss the finding that was just confirmed. We set retain_async=False on every client.retain() call so verdicts, pipeline notes, and stakeholder preferences are immediately searchable:

self.client.retain(
    bank_id=self.bank_id,
    content=(
        f"In {week} for the {region} region, the confirmed root cause of the revenue anomaly "
        f"was {confirmed_cause} (Impact: {dollar_impact}). "
        f"Ruled-out hypotheses: {', '.join(ruled_out) if ruled_out else 'None'}."
    ),
    context=f"investigation_verdict:{region}",
    timestamp=datetime.now(timezone.utc),
    metadata={"region": region, "week": week, "verdict": "confirmed"},
    retain_async=False,
)

Concrete Results: 5-Run Progression and Memory On vs. Off

To verify that every behavioral change comes strictly from stored memories, we ran a five-investigation progression starting from an empty memory bank:

Run Scenario & Stakeholder Recalled Memories Tools Executed (In Order) Tools Count Result & Behavior
Run 1 W10 South (-18%) — Finance Head 0 (Cold Start) holiday -> competitor -> inventory -> pricing -> etl 5 / 5 Finds 20% discount tier (-$42,500). Retains verdict + Finance Head's 1-line rule.
Run 2 W11-Mon South (-64%) — Senior Analyst 2 pricing -> etl 2 / 5 Discovers etl_sales_sync stalled at 02:00 UTC ($0 real loss). Retains ETL lag warning.
Run 3 W11 North (-24%) — Senior Analyst 3 etl -> pricing -> inventory -> competitor -> holiday 5 / 5 Confirms ENT-GATEWAY-02 stockout (-$31,200); explicitly rules out competitor promo & holiday.
Run 4 W12 South (-15%) — Senior Analyst 5 etl -> pricing 2 / 5 Verifies ETL clean first, then catches reactivated SOUTH-Q1-25 promo (-$36,800).
Run 5 (Memory ON) W13 South (-19%) — Finance Head 6 check_etl_pipeline -> check_pricing_changes 2 / 5 Skips holiday, competitor, and inventory. Returns strict 1-line executive summary.
Run 5 (Memory OFF) W13 South (-19%) — Finance Head 0 (Bypassed) holiday -> competitor -> inventory -> pricing -> etl 5 / 5 Reverts to running all 5 checks blindly and returns a generic multi-paragraph breakdown.

On Run 5 with Memory ON, WhyDesk recalls the two prior South pricing anomalies, the W11 Monday ETL stall warning, and the Finance Head formatting preference. It checks check_etl_pipeline first, checks check_pricing_changes second, skips the three ruled-out checks, and outputs:

W13 South revenue dropped 19% (-$47,900 WoW) due to a regional reseller contract repricing that reduced unit ACV; ETL sync verified clean.

Lessons Learned

  1. Synchronous retention (retain_async=False) eliminates race conditions in sequential debugging: When analysts run back-to-back diagnostic queries, waiting for synchronous indexing guarantees that a pipeline warning discovered in one turn immediately protects the next turn.
  2. Retaining falsified hypotheses is just as valuable as retaining root causes: Explicitly recording that competitor promos and holidays were ruled out in a region gives the planner the signal it needs to deprioritize noisy checks.
  3. LLM tool-calling needs deterministic schema repair and numeric validation: Fast inference models occasionally emit malformed tool call payloads or round currency figures in prose. Adding a fallback chain (qwen/qwen3-32b -> openai/gpt-oss-120b -> llama-3.3-70b-versatile) and verifying that every dollar figure in the final response matches the raw tool output kept financial reporting accurate.
  4. Separate data-pipeline health from domain anomalies: Storing ETL stalls as experience memories forced the agent to verify data freshness before blaming pricing or sales execution.

Frontend.title: I Ran the Same Coding Task Through 3 Local LLMs — the Free One on My Laptop Won Twice
Frontend.summary:
I spent a Saturday afternoon doing something deeply unproductive on paper: I ran the same three coding tasks through three local models on my own laptop, and timed everything. No cloud, no API key, no subscription. Just a mid-range machine, a fan that sounded like a hairdryer, and a spreadsheet.
The question I actually wanted answered: can a free model sitting on your own disk do real work, or is local AI still a toy you show your friends?

The setup

Three models, all open-weight, all run through Ollama on the same laptop (16GB RAM, no dedicated GPU — the machine I actually own, not the one in a benchmark blog post):

  • A 7B general coding model
  • A 14B model, the biggest that fits without the laptop giving up
  • A small 3B model I expected to lose Three tasks, the kind I do every week:
  • Write a Python function that parses a messy CSV and returns clean rows, skipping bad lines instead of crashing.
  • Explain a 60-line function I wrote six months ago and forgot.
  • Find the bug in a JavaScript fetch call that works on my machine and fails in production. Each model got the exact same prompt, once. No retries, no cherry-picking. If it failed, it failed. ## What happened Task 1, the CSV parser. The 7B model wrote clean code on the first try, with a proper try/except around the bad rows. The 14B model wrote fancier code — a whole class, type hints, a docstring longer than the function — and it had a bug in it. The 3B model wrote something that worked but silently dropped the header row. Score: 7B wins, 14B second, 3B last. Task 2, explaining my old code. The 14B model won this one easily. It caught that the function was doing two jobs and said so, in plain language. The 7B gave a correct but shallow summary. The 3B model described what the code did line by line, which is the least useful kind of explanation. Score: 14B wins. Task 3, the fetch bug. This one surprised me. The bug was a missing await before a .json() call, plus a CORS header the production server strips. The 7B model spotted both. The 14B spotted the await and missed the header. The 3B model blamed the API key, which was wrong and would have sent me down a two-hour rabbit hole. Score: 7B wins again. Final tally: the 7B model won twice, the 14B won once, the 3B won nothing. The free model on my laptop beat the bigger free model on my laptop most of the time. ## The part nobody mentions: speed The 14B model took about 40 seconds per answer. The 7B took 12. The 3B took 5. That gap matters more than the quality gap, because a 40-second wait breaks your flow. You tab away, you check a message, you lose the thread. Twelve seconds is a pause. Forty seconds is a context switch. So the real ranking, for actual daily work on this machine, is not quality alone. It is quality divided by waiting time. And on that score the 7B model laps the field. ## What I would actually do with this I am not deleting my cloud subscription. For a gnarly refactor or a design question, the big cloud models are still better, and pretending otherwise would be dishonest. But for the everyday stuff — write this parser, explain this function, find this bug — the local model is now good enough, and it has three advantages the cloud does not: it costs nothing per prompt, it never sends my code to anyone's server, and it works on a plane. Here is the honest setup I landed on: local 7B model as the default for small tasks, cloud model for the hard ones. The switch is a habit, not a tool. When I catch myself pasting code into a chat window for something small, I stop and ask the local model first. Half the time it is done before the cloud tab would have finished loading. If you have a laptop with 16GB of RAM, try it. Install Ollama, pull a 7B coding model, and give it one real task from your actual work — not a demo prompt, a real one. Time it. Then decide whether the cloud deserves to be your first stop, or just your second. The fan noise is the price of admission. Worth it.

Frontend.title: I ran two OCR engines and a BERT model entirely in the browser — here's what I learned
Frontend.summary:
Every day, someone pastes a dashboard screenshot into Slack, a Jira ticket, or a slide deck with customer names, emails, and revenue figures still perfectly readable. The usual fix is a redaction tool — and almost every redaction tool uploads your screenshot to a server, which is exactly the thing you were trying to avoid.

So I built VaultSnip: a free, open-source tool that finds and blurs sensitive text in screenshots. The constraint I set myself: everything runs on your device. No backend, no account, no upload. The whole app is static files on Cloudflare Pages; your screenshot never leaves the browser tab.

That constraint forced me to run a full ML pipeline client-side. Here's what that actually took.

The pipeline: two OCR engines and a PII model, all in the tab

To decide what to blur, you first need to know what text is in the image and where. VaultSnip layers three engines, each running in a Web Worker:

  1. Tesseract.js does the fast first pass. Masks land in a few seconds, so the user sees results immediately.
  2. PP-OCRv5 (PaddleOCR's mobile detection + recognition models, as ONNX) catches what Tesseract misses — small print, low-contrast labels, text inside chart chrome. I run the official ONNX exports through ONNX Runtime Web and wrote the DB post-processing and CTC decoding myself in TypeScript.
  3. A BERT-small PII model (int8-quantized ONNX, via Transformers.js) classifies the recognized text: is this a person's name, an email, an ID, a company? That decides what gets masked versus left alone.

A design rule that mattered more than any model choice: later passes only ever add masks, never remove them. The user watches the screenshot get progressively safer, and an engine disagreement can't un-redact something.

Lesson 1: cross-origin isolation is the real price of admission

ONNX Runtime Web's threaded SIMD build needs SharedArrayBuffer, and browsers only give you that when the page is cross-origin isolated — Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin and Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp headers on everything.

That sounds like two lines of config. In practice it means every resource you load — every script, every wasm file, every model weight — must either be same-origin or explicitly opt in. It shaped the entire architecture: all models are bundled and served from the same origin, nothing is pulled from a CDN at runtime.

Which turned out to be a feature. "No requests to third-party servers" stopped being a promise and became something you can verify in the Network tab.

Lesson 2: model size is a UX problem, not a bandwidth problem

The int8-quantized BERT is small by ML standards, and the PP-OCRv5 mobile models are a few megabytes each, gzipped. Users will wait for that once — if the app is honest about it and useful before the download finishes.

That's why the layering matters: Tesseract.js (which is comparatively tiny) delivers first masks in seconds while the heavier models are still warming up. The slow part runs while the user is already getting value.

Lesson 3: measure what you miss, and publish it

Any detection pipeline misses things. Most tools in this space deal with that by never mentioning it.

I went the other way: the repo has an automated benchmark that renders fictional dashboards, runs the full pipeline, and measures exactly how much readable text area survives unmasked. Right now that's about 0.25% of readable area, and the number is published in the repo's ACCURACY.md, failure cases included.

This felt risky ("my tool's README admits it's imperfect!") and has been nothing but positive. Users trust a published ~ 0.2% far more than an implied 0%, and the benchmark doubles as a regression gate in CI — no change ships if the number gets worse.

Lesson 4: the replica — editing pixels in place

Blurring is fine for chat, but sometimes you need a screenshot that still looks real — for a demo, a tutorial, a portfolio. VaultSnip's "replica" mode replaces each sensitive value, in place, with a synthetic one: same position, same font size, same color and alignment, with plausible fake data (via Faker, also running locally).

The hard rule, enforced by a pixel-diff e2e test: zero changed pixels outside the replaced text boxes. No redrawing charts, no reconstructed layouts. A bar-chart edge that runs through a text box survives the replacement. The replica is the original image, surgically edited — which is the only way it stays believable.

What it became

What started as a web page is now also a Chrome/Edge extension (same pipeline, plus one-key blurring of charts on live pages) and a Windows desktop app (Tauri 2, with a global hotkey that snips any screen region straight into the masker). All of it Apache-2.0, all of it offline-capable.

TypeScript.title: Find which prospects run Shopify, HubSpot or Microsoft 365, from a list of domains
TypeScript.summary:
A lot of B2B selling starts with "what do they run?". A Shopify app developer wants the stores on Shopify, an agency wants the sites with no ad pixel, an email security vendor wants the companies on Microsoft 365 without a DMARC policy. The answer is sitting in each company's homepage and DNS records; reading it for a few thousand domains by hand is the problem.

This post turns a domain list into a segmented prospect sheet in Python, then compares the tech stack lookup tools on the Apify Store using the prices their Store pages listed at the time of writing.

Disclosure: I'm Aurelix, and I built the Tech Stack API. It's a paid tool (prices below). Check each Store page before you buy: prices change.

What one row tells you

Each domain is read live: its homepage once (robots.txt obeyed) and its public MX, SPF, DMARC and NS records. One row per domain:

  • One column per category, as a list of names: cms, ecommerce, analytics, tag_manager, advertising (Meta Pixel, Google Ads, LinkedIn, TikTok...), chat, crm_marketing, payments, consent, framework, backend, web_server, cdn_hosting.
  • Email from DNS: email_provider (Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, Zoho...), email_security (a gateway such as Mimecast or Proofpoint), email_sender (sending services named in SPF), dmarc_policy (none, quarantine or reject), plus the raw mx and spf.
  • dns_provider, technologies (every detection as name and category), homepage_checked, and a note when the homepage could not be read.

When a site blocks bots, the row still carries the DNS fields, which is often enough to segment by email provider.

From a domain list to segments 

pip install apify-client

import csv
import os
from collections import Counter

from apify_client import ApifyClient

DOMAINS = ["allbirds.com", "davidstea.com", "webflow.com", "hubspot.com", "mcgill.ca", "wordpress.org"]

client = ApifyClient(os.environ["APIFY_TOKEN"])
run = client.actor("aurelix/tech-stack-detector").call(run_input={"domains": DOMAINS})
rows = list(client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items())

cols = ["domain", "cms", "ecommerce", "analytics", "advertising", "chat", "crm_marketing",
        "email_provider", "email_security", "dmarc_policy", "homepage_checked", "note"]
with open("stacks.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    w = csv.writer(f)
    w.writerow(cols)
    for r in rows:
        w.writerow(["; ".join(r[c]) if isinstance(r[c], list) else r[c] for c in cols])

shopify = [r["domain"] for r in rows if "Shopify" in r["ecommerce"]]
no_pixel = [r["domain"] for r in rows if r["homepage_checked"] and not r["advertising"]]
weak_dmarc = [r["domain"] for r in rows if r["email_provider"] and r["dmarc_policy"] in (None, "none")]
print("On Shopify:", shopify)
print("No ad pixel on the homepage:", no_pixel)
print("Email provider found, DMARC missing or monitor-only:", weak_dmarc)
print("Email providers:", Counter(r["email_provider"] or "unknown" for r in rows).most_common())

Each segment is a different conversation: Shopify stores for an app or agency, sites with no ad pixel for a paid-ads pitch, a missing or monitor-only DMARC policy for an email security vendor. homepage_checked matters for the second one: an empty advertising list only means "none found" when the homepage was actually read.

Where the domains come from:

  • Your CRM or a purchased list: paste the domains or full URLs; only the host is used, so https://apify.com/store and APIFY.COM count as one domain.
  • A local business list: run the Google Maps Phone Scraper for a category and city; its website column is this tool's domains input, and cms then shows who is on Wix, Squarespace or WordPress.

Tech stack lookup tools on the Apify Store compared

Prices per 1,000 domains from each Store page at the time of writing:

Free plan $1.50 $2.00 $0.24 $10.00 per site with a detection
Bronze $1.05 $2.00 $0.21 $10.00
Gold $1.05 $2.00 $0.13 $10.00
Start fee per run $0.001 none $0.005 none
Where the data comes from live homepage + DNS BuiltWith's own database live pages, 1 to 5 per domain live site
Email provider (MX), SPF senders, DMARC policy yes not stated not stated not stated
One column per category yes not stated flat list of categories not stated
Confidence and evidence per detection no not stated yes not stated
Unreachable domains free yes not stated not stated yes

Where each wins: automation-lab is far cheaper per domain than any of the others, can read several pages per domain, and gives a confidence score and the evidence behind each match; for bulk enrichment of technology names alone, it's the one to try first. BuiltWith's official tool is the most used and draws on BuiltWith's own database rather than a single live visit. scrapemint charges only for sites where it found something. The Aurelix tool fits when the email side matters as much as the website: mailbox provider, security gateway, SPF senders and DMARC policy from DNS on every row, in flat CRM-ready columns, still filled in when the homepage blocks bots.

Limits

  • Homepage only, no JavaScript. Tools loaded later by a tag manager, only on inner pages, or only after cookie consent can be missed. Tag managers themselves are detected.
  • No history. No first-seen dates or spend estimates; each run is a fresh read, and there is no change-only mode.
  • Rule-based detection from our own fingerprint rules (not Wappalyzer or BuiltWith data); a rare false match or miss is possible, and versions are not reported.
  • SPF is read one level deep: includes are matched by name, nested includes and redirects are not followed.
  • Blocked sites get the DNS fields only, with homepage_checked false and a note saying why.
  • Speed: ten domains at a time, about 40 to 60 a minute; for lists above about 2,500 domains, raise the run timeout.

Cost

You pay per domain analysed. A domain whose homepage is blocked is still charged once, because its row carries the DNS fields; domains that neither resolve nor answer, and duplicates in the input, are free. The current price per domain is on the Store page; Apify's free plan includes $5 of credit a month, enough for a few thousand domains.

TypeScript.title: I Ran the Same Coding Task Through 3 Local LLMs — the Free One on My Laptop Won Twice
TypeScript.summary:
I spent a Saturday afternoon doing something deeply unproductive on paper: I ran the same three coding tasks through three local models on my own laptop, and timed everything. No cloud, no API key, no subscription. Just a mid-range machine, a fan that sounded like a hairdryer, and a spreadsheet.
The question I actually wanted answered: can a free model sitting on your own disk do real work, or is local AI still a toy you show your friends?

The setup

Three models, all open-weight, all run through Ollama on the same laptop (16GB RAM, no dedicated GPU — the machine I actually own, not the one in a benchmark blog post):

  • A 7B general coding model
  • A 14B model, the biggest that fits without the laptop giving up
  • A small 3B model I expected to lose Three tasks, the kind I do every week:
  • Write a Python function that parses a messy CSV and returns clean rows, skipping bad lines instead of crashing.
  • Explain a 60-line function I wrote six months ago and forgot.
  • Find the bug in a JavaScript fetch call that works on my machine and fails in production. Each model got the exact same prompt, once. No retries, no cherry-picking. If it failed, it failed. ## What happened Task 1, the CSV parser. The 7B model wrote clean code on the first try, with a proper try/except around the bad rows. The 14B model wrote fancier code — a whole class, type hints, a docstring longer than the function — and it had a bug in it. The 3B model wrote something that worked but silently dropped the header row. Score: 7B wins, 14B second, 3B last. Task 2, explaining my old code. The 14B model won this one easily. It caught that the function was doing two jobs and said so, in plain language. The 7B gave a correct but shallow summary. The 3B model described what the code did line by line, which is the least useful kind of explanation. Score: 14B wins. Task 3, the fetch bug. This one surprised me. The bug was a missing await before a .json() call, plus a CORS header the production server strips. The 7B model spotted both. The 14B spotted the await and missed the header. The 3B model blamed the API key, which was wrong and would have sent me down a two-hour rabbit hole. Score: 7B wins again. Final tally: the 7B model won twice, the 14B won once, the 3B won nothing. The free model on my laptop beat the bigger free model on my laptop most of the time. ## The part nobody mentions: speed The 14B model took about 40 seconds per answer. The 7B took 12. The 3B took 5. That gap matters more than the quality gap, because a 40-second wait breaks your flow. You tab away, you check a message, you lose the thread. Twelve seconds is a pause. Forty seconds is a context switch. So the real ranking, for actual daily work on this machine, is not quality alone. It is quality divided by waiting time. And on that score the 7B model laps the field. ## What I would actually do with this I am not deleting my cloud subscription. For a gnarly refactor or a design question, the big cloud models are still better, and pretending otherwise would be dishonest. But for the everyday stuff — write this parser, explain this function, find this bug — the local model is now good enough, and it has three advantages the cloud does not: it costs nothing per prompt, it never sends my code to anyone's server, and it works on a plane. Here is the honest setup I landed on: local 7B model as the default for small tasks, cloud model for the hard ones. The switch is a habit, not a tool. When I catch myself pasting code into a chat window for something small, I stop and ask the local model first. Half the time it is done before the cloud tab would have finished loading. If you have a laptop with 16GB of RAM, try it. Install Ollama, pull a 7B coding model, and give it one real task from your actual work — not a demo prompt, a real one. Time it. Then decide whether the cloud deserves to be your first stop, or just your second. The fan noise is the price of admission. Worth it.

Rust.title: Treat a crawler skill's output as a versioned interface
Rust.summary:
A saved crawler workflow is easier to reuse when the next person can trust its output shape. Finding the same button again is only part of the job. Downstream code still needs stable field names, clear missing values, and a way to distinguish a complete collection from an interrupted one.

Here is a small contract I would put around a reusable extraction skill. It is an application-side design example, not a BrowserAct API, a generated Skill Forge artifact, or a claim that a real website passed these checks. This article comes from the BrowserAct team.

Write the consumer's assumptions first

Start with the code or person receiving the result. Which fields identify a row? Which values may be absent? What does the caller do when pagination stops early?

For a directory collection, a consumer might require a source-specific record ID and a source URL. A contact email could remain null when it was not visible. The workflow should not invent a value simply because an export column exists.

Decide those rules before saving the skill. Otherwise a changed extraction path can return plausible JSON that quietly breaks an importer.

Separate shape from coverage

Consider this fictional response:

{
  "schema_version": "records.v1",
  "stop_reason": "row_limit",
  "rows": [
    {
      "record_id": "demo-17",
      "source_url": "https://example.com/records/demo-17",
      "email": null
    }
  ]
}

The response can be structurally valid while covering only part of the requested data. A row limit is an intentional stop, not proof that the directory ended. A blocked page is another reason to return a partial collection with an explicit status.

Use a separate coverage check when you have an authoritative expected set. Without that set, report what was observed and how traversal ended. Do not infer completeness from the absence of an exception.

Put a small validator at the boundary

The following Python example checks a deliberately narrow contract. It does not fetch a website, validate that a URL belongs to the requested source, or prove that row values are true.

def validate_result(result):
    if not isinstance(result, dict):
        raise ValueError("result must be an object")
    if result.get("schema_version") != "records.v1":
        raise ValueError("unsupported schema version")
    if result.get("stop_reason") not in {
        "exhausted", "row_limit", "blocked"
    }:
        raise ValueError("unknown stop reason")
    rows = result.get("rows")
    if not isinstance(rows, list):
        raise ValueError("rows must be a list")
    seen = set()
    for index, row in enumerate(rows):
        if not isinstance(row, dict):
            raise ValueError(f"row {index} must be an object")
        for field in ("record_id", "source_url"):
            value = row.get(field)
            if not isinstance(value, str) or not value.strip():
                raise ValueError(f"row {index}: missing {field}")
        key = row["record_id"].strip()
        if key in seen:
            raise ValueError(f"duplicate record_id: {key}")
        seen.add(key)
    return result

Here, IDs are unique within this one result. A cross-source collection would need a key that includes the source identity. Do not copy this deduplication rule into a different dataset without checking what makes a record unique.

The validator permits additional fields so optional additions do not automatically break this consumer. It also permits an empty list. Whether an empty collection is an acceptable business result belongs in the coverage and acceptance rules, not in a guessed minimum row count.

Test the contract without pretending to test the crawler

Before connecting it to an importer, try synthetic fixtures: a valid response, a partial blocked response, an empty response, a duplicate ID, a missing source URL, an unsupported version, and a non-list rows value.

The last four should be rejected by this validator. The first three should pass shape validation, with their different business meanings preserved. Passing these fixtures establishes the behavior of this local check. It says nothing about browser access, pagination correctness, or extraction accuracy on a live portal.

Then test the actual saved skill separately, with authorized access and new inputs. Inspect source evidence as well as the returned structure. Keep those results distinct from the synthetic checks.

Version meaning changes, not only field names

A change from a local record ID to a global identifier may keep the same JSON type while changing the meaning. Changing a date from local time to UTC can do the same thing. Treat those changes as contract decisions.

Record the skill revision and contract version with each run. When introducing a breaking change, retain a representative old result and exercise the migration before replacing the importer. A version label is useful only when consumers actually check it.

For missing optional values, document whether null means not observed, unavailable, or not applicable. If your business needs those distinctions, add a separate status field rather than overloading null with several incompatible meanings.

Our Skill Forge workflow guide discusses turning exploration into something reusable. An output contract gives the next caller a concrete boundary to review, even when the website path changes.

Which breaks your downstream pipeline more often: changed fields, duplicate records, or an incomplete collection that looked successful?

Rust.title: My Analytics Agent Stopped Repeating Its Wrong Guesses With Hindsight
Rust.summary:
My Analytics Agent Stopped Repeating Its Wrong Guesses With Hindsight

Every Monday morning, someone in leadership asks why a regional revenue metric dropped, and an analyst spends two hours checking the exact same five tables in the exact same order. When we first wired an LLM tool-calling agent to automate root-cause investigations, it had an infuriating habit: it treated every single alert like its first day on the job.

If the South region experienced three consecutive pricing-tier drops over three weeks, a stateless agent would still burn time querying holiday calendars, competitor promo trackers, and warehouse stockout logs before checking pricing. Worse, if the Monday morning ETL sync stalled at 02:00 UTC, the agent would panic over incomplete tables and report a fake revenue collapse. And no matter how many times the Finance Head asked for a single-line summary with the exact dollar variance, the next session returned a multi-paragraph essay.

To fix this, we built WhyDesk—an autonomous metric investigation system powered by FastAPI, Groq tool-calling, and the Hindsight GitHub repository. Instead of treating memory as a passive chat log, we used Vectorize agent memory to dynamically reorder diagnostic tool execution, skip low-probability checks, flag flaky data pipelines before trusting raw numbers, and enforce stakeholder-specific output formatting.

What the System Does and How It Hangs Together

WhyDesk sits between business stakeholders (Finance Head and Senior Analyst) and five deterministic diagnostic tools that inspect weekly regional performance across South, North, West, and East:

  • check_holiday_calendar: Audits regional banking holidays and seasonal B2B checkout dips.
  • check_competitor_promos: Scans market intelligence feeds for aggressive rival discounting.
  • check_inventory_stockouts: Inspects warehouse SKU depletion and unfulfilled hardware bundle backlogs.
  • check_pricing_changes: Audits contract repricing, partner promo codes, discount overrides, and unit ACV shifts.
  • check_etl_pipeline: Verifies warehouse sync completion, job timestamps, and missing row counts.

When an investigation request arrives at POST /api/investigate, WhyDesk does not immediately hand the five tool schemas to the LLM. Instead, it executes a four-stage loop built around the primitives described in what Hindsight does:

User Query + Stakeholder Role
       │
       ▼
1. Hindsight Recall (world, experience, observation) + Reflect
       │
       ▼
2. Memory-Driven Tool Planner (Groq qwen/qwen3-32b -> openai/gpt-oss-120b -> llama-3.3-70b-versatile)
   [Reorders diagnostic tools & enables early stopping once root cause + clean ETL are verified]
       │
       ▼
3. Deterministic Tool Execution + Numeric Grounding Verification
       │
       ▼
4. Synchronous Hindsight Retain (Confirmed cause, ruled-out theories, pipeline reliability, format rule)

Core Technical Story: Turning Memory Into Tool Execution Order

Most agent implementations stuff retrieved text chunks into a prompt and hope the model changes its behavior. In data analysis, passive context is not enough. We needed institutional memory to govern which diagnostic tools run first, which tools get skipped, and how the final answer is shaped.

We organized our Hindsight memory bank (whydesk-bank) around three memory types and configured the bank disposition with high skepticism and literalism (skepticism: 4, literalism: 4, empathy: 2) so confirmed metric verdicts always outweigh unverified guesses:

  1. World facts (world): Confirmed historical root causes and explicitly falsified hypotheses for a region or product line (for example, "In W10 and W12 for the South region, revenue drops were caused by pricing configuration changes; holiday and competitor promo hypotheses were ruled out").
  2. Operational experiences (experience): Lessons learned about data source reliability (for example, "Monday revenue drops in W11 were false alarms caused by an etl_sales_sync warehouse stall; always verify ETL pipeline status before trusting Monday numbers").
  3. Stakeholder observations (observation): Reporting rules per persona (for example, "Stakeholder 'Finance Head' strictly requires a 1-line summary with the exact dollar impact").

1. Pre-Investigation Recall and Reflection (backend/memory.py)

Before calling Groq, WhyDeskMemory.recall_context() queries Hindsight across all three memory types and runs reflect() to synthesize a tactical plan for the current investigation:

def recall_context(self, question: str, region: str, stakeholder: str) -> dict:
    query = (
        f"Past metric investigations for region {region}, reliable vs unreliable data sources, "
        f"ruled out causes, and formatting preferences for stakeholder {stakeholder}. "
        f"Question: {question}"
    )
    recall_resp = self.client.recall(
        bank_id=self.bank_id,
        query=query,
        types=["world", "experience", "observation"],
        budget="mid",
        max_tokens=2048,
    )

    memories = [
        {
            "id": getattr(r, "id", ""),
            "text": getattr(r, "text", ""),
            "type": getattr(r, "type", "world"),
            "context": getattr(r, "context", ""),
        }
        for r in (recall_resp.results or [])
    ]

    reflect_resp = self.client.reflect(
        bank_id=self.bank_id,
        query=(
            f"Based on past investigations in {region} and stakeholder {stakeholder}: "
            f"1) Which diagnostic tools should run first? "
            f"2) Which hypotheses were repeatedly ruled out? "
            f"3) Any data pipeline traps to check first? "
            f"4) How should the final response for {stakeholder} be formatted?"
        ),
        budget="low",
    )

    return {
        "query": query,
        "memories": memories,
        "reflection": getattr(reflect_resp, "text", ""),
    }

2. Memory-Driven Tool Ordering and Early Stopping (backend/agent.py)

Rather than hardcoding regional rules in Python, backend/agent.py derives the diagnostic execution queue strictly from the recalled memory text and reflection output. On a cold start (0 recalled memories) or when the user switches the UI toggle to Memory off, the agent runs all five tools in the default baseline sequence (check_holiday_calendar -> check_competitor_promos -> check_inventory_stockouts -> check_pricing_changes -> check_etl_pipeline).

When Memory on is active and Hindsight returns prior investigations, the planner scores each diagnostic tool based on recalled pipeline warnings, historical regional root causes, and previously ruled-out checks:

def derive_tool_order_from_memory(memories: list[dict], reflection: str) -> list[str]:
    combined = " ".join(m.get("text", "") for m in memories) + " " + (reflection or "")
    text = combined.lower()

    if not text.strip():
        return list(DEFAULT_TOOL_ORDER)

    priority_scores = {tool: 0 for tool in DEFAULT_TOOL_ORDER}

    if "etl" in text or "pipeline" in text or "sync" in text or "lag" in text:
        priority_scores["check_etl_pipeline"] += 30
    if "pricing" in text or "discount" in text or "promo code" in text or "repricing" in text:
        priority_scores["check_pricing_changes"] += 20
    if "stockout" in text or "inventory" in text:
        priority_scores["check_inventory_stockouts"] += 15
    if "ruled out" in text and "holiday" in text:
        priority_scores["check_holiday_calendar"] -= 10
    if "ruled out" in text and "competitor" in text:
        priority_scores["check_competitor_promos"] -= 10

    return sorted(
        DEFAULT_TOOL_ORDER,
        key=lambda t: (-priority_scores[t], DEFAULT_TOOL_ORDER.index(t)),
    )

Once the prioritized tools run, the agent checks whether the warehouse ETL sync is verified clean and a primary anomaly (status == "anomaly_detected") has been isolated. When both conditions are met under memory-guided execution, the loop stops early and skips the remaining low-probability checks.

3. Synchronous Post-Investigation Retention (backend/memory.py)

In an interactive analytics workflow, an analyst often runs follow-up investigations seconds apart. If memory ingestion happens asynchronously in the background, the very next query might miss the finding that was just confirmed. We set retain_async=False on every client.retain() call so verdicts, pipeline notes, and stakeholder preferences are immediately searchable:

self.client.retain(
    bank_id=self.bank_id,
    content=(
        f"In {week} for the {region} region, the confirmed root cause of the revenue anomaly "
        f"was {confirmed_cause} (Impact: {dollar_impact}). "
        f"Ruled-out hypotheses: {', '.join(ruled_out) if ruled_out else 'None'}."
    ),
    context=f"investigation_verdict:{region}",
    timestamp=datetime.now(timezone.utc),
    metadata={"region": region, "week": week, "verdict": "confirmed"},
    retain_async=False,
)

Concrete Results: 5-Run Progression and Memory On vs. Off

To verify that every behavioral change comes strictly from stored memories, we ran a five-investigation progression starting from an empty memory bank:

Run Scenario & Stakeholder Recalled Memories Tools Executed (In Order) Tools Count Result & Behavior
Run 1 W10 South (-18%) — Finance Head 0 (Cold Start) holiday -> competitor -> inventory -> pricing -> etl 5 / 5 Finds 20% discount tier (-$42,500). Retains verdict + Finance Head's 1-line rule.
Run 2 W11-Mon South (-64%) — Senior Analyst 2 pricing -> etl 2 / 5 Discovers etl_sales_sync stalled at 02:00 UTC ($0 real loss). Retains ETL lag warning.
Run 3 W11 North (-24%) — Senior Analyst 3 etl -> pricing -> inventory -> competitor -> holiday 5 / 5 Confirms ENT-GATEWAY-02 stockout (-$31,200); explicitly rules out competitor promo & holiday.
Run 4 W12 South (-15%) — Senior Analyst 5 etl -> pricing 2 / 5 Verifies ETL clean first, then catches reactivated SOUTH-Q1-25 promo (-$36,800).
Run 5 (Memory ON) W13 South (-19%) — Finance Head 6 check_etl_pipeline -> check_pricing_changes 2 / 5 Skips holiday, competitor, and inventory. Returns strict 1-line executive summary.
Run 5 (Memory OFF) W13 South (-19%) — Finance Head 0 (Bypassed) holiday -> competitor -> inventory -> pricing -> etl 5 / 5 Reverts to running all 5 checks blindly and returns a generic multi-paragraph breakdown.

On Run 5 with Memory ON, WhyDesk recalls the two prior South pricing anomalies, the W11 Monday ETL stall warning, and the Finance Head formatting preference. It checks check_etl_pipeline first, checks check_pricing_changes second, skips the three ruled-out checks, and outputs:

W13 South revenue dropped 19% (-$47,900 WoW) due to a regional reseller contract repricing that reduced unit ACV; ETL sync verified clean.

Lessons Learned

  1. Synchronous retention (retain_async=False) eliminates race conditions in sequential debugging: When analysts run back-to-back diagnostic queries, waiting for synchronous indexing guarantees that a pipeline warning discovered in one turn immediately protects the next turn.
  2. Retaining falsified hypotheses is just as valuable as retaining root causes: Explicitly recording that competitor promos and holidays were ruled out in a region gives the planner the signal it needs to deprioritize noisy checks.
  3. LLM tool-calling needs deterministic schema repair and numeric validation: Fast inference models occasionally emit malformed tool call payloads or round currency figures in prose. Adding a fallback chain (qwen/qwen3-32b -> openai/gpt-oss-120b -> llama-3.3-70b-versatile) and verifying that every dollar figure in the final response matches the raw tool output kept financial reporting accurate.
  4. Separate data-pipeline health from domain anomalies: Storing ETL stalls as experience memories forced the agent to verify data freshness before blaming pricing or sales execution.

Rust.title: I made three AI seats argue over the spec before any code. Here's what 10 runs showed.
Rust.summary:
Most of the bad code I've gotten from coding agents wasn't badly written. It was the right code for the wrong plan. The agent misread the task, assumed something about the repo that wasn't true, and then executed that assumption very well.

So I built a tool that spends its effort before the code. It's called Open Council. Three seats argue over a PRD until they all sign off on the same document:

  • Lead PM writes the brief and the PRD.
  • Chief Engineer checks every claim against the real code. Every objection has to cite a file:line.
  • Chief Architect rules on deadlocks and reviews the agreed document. It runs with no tools, so it judges the text, not the repo.

When all three sign off, I approve the PRD with a token. Only then does the Engineer implement it, in an isolated clone. The harness runs the project's gates (its real test commands) and opens a PR only if they pass. Anything else ends as BLOCKED or STALLED, never DONE.

Last week I had ten councils run on version 0.2.1 to see how this holds up. Here's what happened, including the parts that didn't work.

The setup

All ten ran in solo mode, which means every seat is Claude Code (Lead PM on Sonnet, Chief Engineer on Opus, Chief Architect on Sonnet with tools off). They used the quick profile, with at most 4 rounds. The targets were local copies of two small repos: a toy slugify library I keep for testing, and Open Council itself. Local copies have no GitHub remote, so no run could open a PR. That last step ends BLOCKED by design.

# Task Outcome Rounds Minutes
1 slugify: empty string + accents signed off, gate passed 4 6.6
2 gates --json signed off, gate passed 4 6.8
3 gate recipes for Python, Go, Rust signed off, gate passed 3 7.3
4 slugify: maxLength STALLED 4 6.2
5 slugify: empty + accents (repeat) signed off, gate passed 3 4.2
6 gates --json (repeat) STALLED 4 7.2
7 slugify: ß ø æ œ đ ł þ signed off, gate failed, BLOCKED 2 3.4
8 slugify: maxLength (repeat) signed off, gate passed 4 6.3
9 gate recipes (repeat) signed off, gate passed 4 9.2
10 slugify: empty + accents (repeat) signed off, gate passed 2 3.1

8 of 10 signed off. 7 of those 8 passed their gate. The median time to a sign-off or a stall was 6.5 minutes.

The catch nobody asked for

Six of the runs were on the slugify repo. In all six, the Chief Engineer's first objection had nothing to do with the task.

The repo's package.json had "test": "node --test test/". On Node 22 that argument is read as a module path, not a folder, so npm test ran 0 of the 2 existing tests. It had been quietly broken since before I started. No task mentioned it.

In run 1 the Engineer reproduced it, tried two working alternatives, and made fixing the test script the first commit of the plan. Its reasoning was simple: you can't claim the new tests pass if the runner doesn't run tests.

This is the thing I wanted from the design. A single agent asked to "handle empty strings in slugify" would most likely write the fix and the tests and report that they pass. A seat whose only job is to check claims against the repo found that the claim couldn't be checked at all.

What went wrong

Two runs stalled, and the same way. In both, the Engineer had no objections left. Then the Architect raised one more concern. In run 4 it asked for a README line the task never mentioned. The revision that answered it introduced a new problem: one of the new assertions would fail on a correct implementation. The Engineer objected in the last round, the budget ran out, and nothing reached me for approval. The harness wrote the last draft and the open objections to a file and stopped.

A stall is the system working, because nothing wrong got built. But two stalls with the same shape tell me the Architect's late concerns cost more than they're worth. I already made one change for this: a concern that could have been raised in an earlier round is waived on a resubmission. These two runs show it isn't enough yet.

One run was blocked by its own plan. In run 7 the council agreed on a plan and named its own test command, node --test test/slug.test.js. But the project config runs npm test, which was still broken in that repo, and the Architect had ruled that fixing package.json was out of scope. So execution ran the configured gate, it failed, and the run ended BLOCKED. Nothing was pushed. The code itself passed the plan's own 7 tests when I checked afterwards.

The harness did the right thing by not calling it done. The real bug is that a PRD can name a gate the project doesn't run, and nothing flags that before execution. That's an open issue now.

Solo mode isn't the real test. Every seat in these runs was the same model family. The point of separate seats is that they don't share blind spots, and the council is designed to put Claude, Gemini and Grok in different seats. I haven't run that mixed setup enough to say whether it catches more. Ten runs on two small repos, with three tasks repeated, is a smoke test, not a rate.

What I took from it

  1. Review the plan, not just the diff. The most useful objection in these runs was about the repo's state, not the task. It only came up because a seat was told to check claims against the code before anyone wrote any.
  2. Make "done" something the harness checks, not something the agent says. Run 7 had passing code and still ended BLOCKED, because the gate the project actually runs failed. I'd rather read a BLOCKED than find out later.
  3. Publish the failures. The stalls taught me more than the sign-offs, and they're the part I'd want to see before trusting a tool like this.

Trying it

You need Node 18 or later, macOS or Linux, and Claude Code. In a git repo:

npm install -g open-council-cli
council init --solo
council doctor
council backlog add "your task here" --priority 1
SESSION=$(council open my-task --item 001)
council deliberate "$SESSION"

When it signs off, it prints the PRD's path and the exact council approve command. That step is yours to run. Then council handoff "$SESSION" and council run "$SESSION" implement it and open the PR.

The code, and full replays of these runs with every objection, are at https://github.com/goshtasb/OpenCouncil. It's MIT licensed. If you run a council and it stalls or ships something wrong, that's the report I'd most like to read.

This article was written with the help of AI, and the ten runs were driven by an AI agent on my behalf. I checked the numbers against the run logs before publishing.
