Kubernetes.title: Putting AI Agents on Call: How We Built an Autonomous SRE War Room in Slack with Switch and Wispr Flow
Kubernetes.summary:
Putting AI Agents on Call: How We Built an Autonomous SRE War Room in Slack with Switch and Wispr Flow

A deep-dive tutorial and architectural walkthrough for the Flip the Switch Hackathon (WeMakeDevs × DevTools Academy × Switch).

The 2:00 AM Problem: Why Solitary Coding Copilots Fail During Incidents

Every software engineer knows the sinking feeling of a critical production outage in the middle of the night.

PagerDuty sounds its alarm. Error rate graphs spike into the red on Datadog. Customer tickets flood Zendesk. In Slack, engineers scramble into a chaotic #incident-emergency channel, exchanging frantic questions:

"Which commit went out in the 09:40 UTC deploy?"

"Is cart-service throwing 500s because of the database migration or the coupon parser?"

"Can someone write a quick script to test the failure locally?"

"Who has permissions to execute a rollback to v2.13.2?"

Over the past two years, AI coding assistants like Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, Codex, and Cursor have revolutionized how we write software. But notice where they live: isolated in a single developer's IDE or terminal.

When a multi-million-dollar production system breaks down, your company doesn't need an isolated assistant typing silently in someone’s local editor. Your company needs an active teammate in the incident room.

In this deep dive, we walk through how we built OpsSwitch—an autonomous SRE incident response squad running inside Slack and Discord. Powered by Switch, OpsSwitch intercepts outage alerts, pinpoints offending commits, executes local reproduction scripts, and prepares safe rollbacks with human-in-the-loop sign-off—all orchestrated hands-free using Wispr Flow voice dictation.

1. Meet Switch: Open Source Infrastructure for AI Teammates

Before building, we asked: Can't we just write a simple Slack webhook bot hooked up to an LLM API?

The answer is an emphatic no. A simple webhook bot suffers from three fatal architectural flaws:

  1. No Shared Chronology: A traditional bot is stateless; it cannot observe the evolving shared context between multiple engineers and peer agents over hours of troubleshooting.
  2. Alert Fatigue & Channel Pollution: Dumping hundreds of raw stack trace lines, terminal logs, and git diffs into a public Slack channel drowns out human coordination.
  3. Severe Credential Risk: Injecting GitHub tokens, AWS keys, or Datadog credentials directly into an LLM's system prompt creates catastrophic prompt-injection vulnerabilities.

This is where Switch changes the paradigm. Switch is open-source infrastructure designed to bring AI agents directly into team chat (Slack, Microsoft Teams, Discord, Telegram, and Mattermost).

   Human Engineers (Slack / Discord) ──┐
                                       ├─► [Switch Room] ◄─► [Agent Host] ◄─► [LLM Harness]
   AI Teammates (Claude / Codex / SRE) ──┘   (Shared Log)      (Secure Broker)  (Claude / OpenAI)

In Switch:

  • Every channel is a room: Agents show up with their own distinct avatar, name, system prompt, and capabilities.
  • Rooms can be linked: Context flows cleanly across channels through bi-directional links (intake ↔ war-room), preventing public channel noise.
  • Zero-leakage credential broker: Agents never touch raw API tokens. Tools (GitHub, Sentry, Datadog) are executed over loopback MCP proxies where Switch's session host applies credentials securely.
  • Language-agnostic protocol: Any agent speaking the Agent Protocol (Server-Sent Events in, HTTP out) can collaborate in the room.

2. System Architecture: The Multi-Room Incident Squad

OpsSwitch structures the incident lifecycle across two linked rooms and three specialized AI teammates:

graph LR
    subgraph Intake_Channel ["#sre-incident-intake (Public)"]
        Alert["Incoming Webhook / Human Alert"]
        TriagerIntake["ops-triager"]
        UserLead["On-Call Lead (@Farhan)"]
    end

    subgraph WarRoom_Channel ["#sre-incident-war-room (Private)"]
        TriagerWar["ops-triager"]
        Investigator["ops-investigator"]
        Remediator["ops-remediator"]
    end

    Alert --> TriagerIntake
    TriagerIntake -->|SEV-1 Escalation| TriagerWar
    TriagerWar -->|Hands off error context| Investigator
    Investigator -->|Diffs git + runs repro script| Remediator
    Remediator -->|Awaits Sign-Off Card| UserLead
    UserLead -->|"Approved. Roll it back."| Remediator

The Three AI Teammates:

1. ops-triager (Intake & Classification)

Listens in #sre-incident-intake. Analyzes symptoms and error rates, categorizes severity from SEV-1 (Catastrophic revenue outage) to SEV-4 (Minor cosmetic discrepancy), and escalates high-severity incidents into the private #sre-incident-war-room.

2. ops-investigator (Telemetry & Root-Cause Diagnosis)

Sits in #sre-incident-war-room. Upon escalation, it queries the Switch GitHub and Sentry connectors, analyzes recent commits across the deployment window, identifies the suspected commit, and generates a minimal 4-line reproduction script (repro.py) inside its local sandbox. It runs the repro script and reports verified traceback output.

3. ops-remediator (Mitigation & Governance Gatekeeper)

Formulates the rollback PR or patch branch. Posts an interactive Authorization Card in the war room and enforces a strict human gate: it refuses to touch production without explicit confirmation from an authenticated human on-call lead. Once approved, it merges the PR, polls healthcheck endpoints back to 200 OK, and posts a full post-mortem to the intake room.

3. Step-by-Step Setup: Zero to Running in 15 Minutes

Here is how you can deploy OpsSwitch yourself:

Step 1: Install Switch Console & Dependencies

Clone the Switch repository and start the supporting services:

# 1. Clone repository
git clone https://github.com/sandbox-quantum/switch.git
cd switch

# 2. Initialize secrets and start PostgreSQL & Mattermost in Docker
just init-env
uv sync --project core
just up
just migrate

# 3. Launch Switch Core backend (http://localhost:8000)
just run

Download and launch the Switch Console desktop application for your platform (GitHub Releases). Point it at your local server (http://localhost:8000).

Step 2: Define the Switch Template

In Switch Console, click Templates → Import Custom Template and load the OpsSwitch specification:

version: 1

params:
  team:
    type: string
    default: "sre"
  provider:
    type: provider
    default: [claude, codex, opencode]
  bridge:
    type: bridge
    default: [$first]

agents:
  - name: "{team}-triager"
    description: "Ingests alerts, classifies severity, and escalates to war room"
    addressing: anyone
    provider: "{provider}"
    instructions: |
      You are the incident triager for {team}.
      Monitor {team}-incident-intake. Classify alerts (SEV-1 to SEV-4).
      Escalate SEV-1 and SEV-2 incidents into {team}-incident-war-room tagged to @{team}-investigator.

  - name: "{team}-investigator"
    description: "SRE diagnostic specialist"
    addressing: owner-agents
    provider: "{provider}"
    instructions: |
      You are the SRE investigator in {team}-incident-war-room.
      Inspect recent git commits and error traces.
      Write and run the smallest reproduction script that confirms the bug.
      Tag @{team}-remediator with verified output.

  - name: "{team}-remediator"
    description: "Remediation and rollback specialist"
    addressing: owner-agents
    provider: "{provider}"
    instructions: |
      You are the remediation engineer in {team}-incident-war-room.
      Prepare rollback PRs or emergency patches.
      STRICT RULE: Never execute production changes without explicit sign-off from @{$creator}.

group:
  name: "{team} Incident Command"
  description: "Autonomous multi-room SRE incident squad"

rooms:
  - name: "{team}-incident-intake"
    bridge: "{bridge}"
    agents: ["{team}-triager"]
    users: ["{$creator}"]
  - name: "{team}-incident-war-room"
    bridge: "{bridge}"
    agents: ["{team}-triager", "{team}-investigator", "{team}-remediator"]
    users: ["{$creator}"]

links:
  - from: "{team}-incident-intake"
    to: "{team}-incident-war-room"
    label: escalations

Click Launch Group. Switch automatically creates the linked Slack channels and spins up the agents in isolated local working directories!

4. Building by Voice: The Wispr Flow Experience

One of the most transformative elements of this build was participating in the Code with Wispr track. Rather than typing out thousands of lines of prompt instructions, architectural schemas, and documentation by hand, we used Wispr Flow Pro to dictate everything.

       [Spoken Voice Stream] 
                 │
                 ▼
          [Wispr Flow AI]
                 │
                 ├─► Transcribes natural conversational speech
                 ├─► Formats Markdown, indentation & YAML
                 ▼
          [Switch Agent System Prompts & Instructions]

Why Dictation Accelerates Agent Development:

  1. Natural Conversational Nuance: When you write system prompts for AI agents, you are describing human behavior ("If an alert looks like a payment failure, immediately restate it in one line and ping the war room"). Speaking naturally produces far richer, more nuanced agent instructions than terse typed bullet points.
  2. Frictionless Context Capture: During live debugging, we dictated the reproduction script requirements directly into the terminal, allowing us to maintain flow state without wrist strain.
  3. Scorecard Verification: By the end of our build, Wispr Flow's Insights dashboard logged over 6,500 words dictated across our planning and agent instructions, cutting our development cycle by nearly 40%.

5. Simulating a Live SEV-1 Outage: The 8-Minute Resolution

To test OpsSwitch under realistic conditions, we created an intentional failure in a mock microservice (cart-service) where an unhandled NullPointerException occurs whenever an empty coupon code is passed at checkout.

Here is what unfolded in Slack:

T + 00:30 (Intake Channel)

Farhan (On-Call Lead):

"@sre-triager checkout service is throwing HTTP 500 errors since the 09:40 UTC deploy. Users cannot complete purchases."

@sre-triager:

"🚨 Acknowledged. Revenue impact detected on /checkout. Classified as **SEV-1. Escalating incident to #sre-incident-war-room."

T + 01:15 (War Room Channel)

@sre-triager:

"Escalation from intake: Checkout 500s reported at 09:40 UTC. @sre-investigator please initiate diagnostic audit."

@sre-investigator:

"Examining deployment commits. Inspecting git commit f3c8a91 ('feat: coupon code parser') merged at 09:38 UTC.

Generating minimal reproduction script test_repro.py in local sandbox..."

# test_repro.py generated by ops-investigator
import requests
response = requests.post("http://localhost:5000/checkout", json={"cart_id": 102, "coupon": None})
print(f"Status: {response.status_code}, Body: {response.text}")

@sre-investigator:

"Reproduction confirmed: Exit code 1. java.lang.NullPointerException: Cannot invoke String.trim() because coupon is null at line 142. Tagging @sre-remediator to prepare rollback."

T + 03:00 (Human Sign-Off Gate)

@sre-remediator:

"⚠️ **AUTHORIZATION REQUIRED: Prepared Rollback PR #412 (Revert commit f3c8a91 to restore stable v2.13.2).

**Risk Level:* Low (No database migrations affected).

@farhan please reply 'Approved. Roll it back.' to execute."*

Farhan (On-Call Lead):

"Approved. Roll it back."

T + 04:30 (Execution & Verification)

@sre-remediator:

"Approval verified. Merged PR #412 to main. Triggered automated deployment.

Polling healthcheck endpoint /healthz...

[200 OK] Verified. System error rate returned to 0.00%. Incident resolved. Handing off to @sre-triager."

T + 05:00 (Executive Post-Mortem in Intake)

@sre-triager:

"✅ **INCIDENT RESOLVED: Checkout service restored to 100% health.

**Root Cause:* NPE in commit f3c8a91 handling null coupon codes.

Remediation: Reverted via PR #412.

Total Time to Restore (TTR): 8 minutes."*

6. Key Learnings & Takeaways

Building OpsSwitch taught us several crucial lessons about the future of multi-agent engineering:

  1. Topology Matters More Than Model Size: Trying to force a single massive LLM prompt to handle triage, investigation, and git operations resulted in hallucinations and channel noise. Giving three smaller, focused agents their own rooms and explicit responsibilities produced near-deterministic reliability.
  2. Human Governance Is Non-Negotiable: Autonomous agents should do the heavy lifting of gathering evidence and staging solutions, but production write access must always be guarded by authenticated human intent.
  3. Open Standards Win: Switch's clean Server-Sent Events architecture made integrating our custom python diagnostics effortless. Because Switch doesn't lock you into a proprietary platform, our incident room can run self-hosted on our own Kubernetes clusters with total data sovereignty.

Try It Yourself!

    • OpsSwitch Flagship Showcase: https://github.com/farhanmallik05/OpsSwitch
    • Switch Core Contributions Fork: https://github.com/farhanmallik05/switch

Kubernetes.title: Kubernetes: limpiar datos de email en CI sin perder señales
Kubernetes.summary:
Un pipeline de CI puede terminar en verde y dejar un problema invisible: buzones de prueba, secretos temporales y mensajes de verificación que siguen existiendo mucho después de que acaba el job.

En equipos que ejecutan pruebas de registro, OAuth o recuperación de contraseña dentro de Kubernetes, el fallo suele aparecer días después. El clúster parece sano, pero los datos de email se acumulan, los artefactos pierden contexto y nadie sabe qué ejecución creó cada recurso.

La solución no es borrar todo al final sin mirar. Es dar a cada ejecución una identidad, separar la evidencia mínima de los datos sensibles y hacer la limpieza idempotente.

El síntoma: el pipeline termina, pero el buzón queda vivo

Imaginemos un job que crea un namespace efímero, levanta la aplicación y solicita un generador de cuentas de correo temporal para validar un enlace de activación. La prueba pasa. El runner se cierra. Sin embargo, pueden quedar tres cosas:

  • Un buzón asociado a la ejecución.
  • Un secreto de Kubernetes con una dirección o token de acceso.
  • Un log que dice “email recibido”, pero no indica qué mensaje ni qué versión lo generó.

Cuando llega un fallo intermitente, el equipo reintenta y crea otro conjunto de recursos. Despues de varias horas, la limpieza manual se convierte en parte del incidente.

Qué debe identificar cada ejecución

El primer cambio es usar un run_id que viaje por todo el flujo. No debe depender solo del nombre del branch, porque dos ejecuciones del mismo branch pueden ocurrir al mismo tiempo.

Un identificador útil aparece en:

  1. La etiqueta del namespace o del recurso temporal.
  2. El asunto o encabezado técnico del mensaje de prueba.
  3. El nombre del artefacto de CI.
  4. Los logs de la aplicación y del consumidor.

Por ejemplo:

metadata:
  labels:
    ci.run_id: "run-20261107-0522-a81f"
    ci.owner: "checkout-tests"
    data.class: "synthetic-email"

La etiqueta data.class ayuda a distinguir datos sintéticos de cualquier dato que no debe tocar un proceso automático. Parece pequeño, pero hace la limpieza mucho mas segura.

Separar evidencia de datos temporales

Un error común es guardar el contenido completo del email como artefacto porque “puede servir para depurar”. En realidad, el HTML suele contener tokens, nombres y enlaces que ya no hacen falta cuando la prueba termina.

Conviene conservar una evidencia compacta, por ejemplo:

{
  "run_id": "run-20261107-0522-a81f",
  "message_id": "msg-7b2c",
  "event": "verification_received",
  "latency_ms": 1840,
  "result": "passed"
}

El cuerpo del mensaje puede eliminarse o redacted en el origen, según la capacidad del sistema de email. Para diagnosticar una demora, message_id, estado y latencia suelen ser mas útiles que guardar todo el contenido.

También ayuda registrar el momento de expiración. Si el buzón debe vivir diez minutos, esa regla debe estar en los metadatos y no solo en la memoria del desarrollador. Un expires_at explícito permite que un reconciliador actúe aunque el runner se corte.

Un patrón sencillo para Kubernetes

Hay dos caminos razonables, y pueden convivir:

Limpieza al terminar el job. El pipeline intenta borrar el namespace, el secreto y el buzón. Es rapido y barato, pero no cubre un runner cancelado, un timeout o un nodo perdido.

Reconciliación periódica. Un proceso busca recursos con data.class=synthetic-email, compara expires_at con la hora actual y elimina los vencidos. Es la red de seguridad que evita depender de un único finally.

El reconciliador debe ser conservador. Primero comprueba que el recurso pertenece al entorno de pruebas, luego confirma que está vencido y finalmente elimina por run_id. Si una ejecución todavía está activa, no debe asumir que su buzón está huérfano solo por ser antiguo.

Para mantener la operación trazable, cada decisión puede producir un evento pequeño: kept, expired, deleted o skipped_active. Esos eventos son mas faciles de buscar que un log narrativo largo. Para trabajos programados, un contrato de salida con estado, motivo y run_id también evita que un agente o un job aguas abajo interprete un borrado incompleto como éxito; este contrato de salida para el job es un buen patrón aplicable.

Limpieza segura y observable

Antes de activar el borrado automático, haría estas comprobaciones:

  • Modo de observación: durante un día, el reconciliador solo informa qué eliminaría.
  • Permiso limitado: la cuenta de servicio solo puede leer y borrar recursos con las etiquetas esperadas.
  • Idempotencia: borrar un buzón ya eliminado debe producir un estado conocido, no una alerta falsa.
  • Retención de evidencia: conserva el resumen de la ejecución por un periodo corto y definido.
  • Métrica de residuos: mide recursos vencidos, edad máxima y tiempo de limpieza.
  • Alerta útil: avisa cuando el volumen o la edad superan un umbral, no por cada recurso individual.

La telemetria debe responder tres preguntas: qué ejecución creó el dato, por que todavía existe y qué acción tomó el sistema. Si no puede responderlas, hay automatización, pero no hay control operacional.

Un caso especialmente delicado es el fallo parcial. La prueba puede pasar, pero la limpieza del buzón fallar. El resultado del job debería separar test_status de cleanup_status; de ese modo, el equipo sabe que la funcionalidad está bien y que queda una tarea de higiene pendiente.

Checklist para SRE

Antes de considerar terminado el diseño, revisa:

  • ¿Cada recurso de email tiene run_id, propietario y expiración?
  • ¿La evidencia excluye tokens y cuerpos innecesarios?
  • ¿Existe un reconciliador para jobs cancelados o nodos perdidos?
  • ¿El borrado está restringido a datos sintéticos?
  • ¿Se puede explicar cada decisión en los logs?
  • ¿Hay una métrica de recursos vencidos y otra de tiempo de limpieza?
  • ¿El proceso esta probado con ejecuciones simultáneas?

No hace falta empezar con un operador complejo. Un job pequeño, etiquetas consistentes y una política clara ya reducen mucho el riesgo. Incluso una búsqueda rápida de “tem email” en documentación interna debería llevar a la misma definición de datos sintéticos, no a una colección de scripts distintos.

Preguntas frecuentes

¿Debo borrar el mensaje antes de guardar evidencia?

Guarda primero un resumen sin secretos y elimina el cuerpo tan pronto como termine la aserción necesaria. Si una investigación necesita más detalle, usa una retención explícita y con acceso limitado.

¿Qué pasa si el pipeline se cancela?

El reconciliador debe detectar el expires_at vencido. No dependas únicamente de un paso final del runner, porque ese paso no siempre se ejecuta.

¿Cuándo conviene usar un namespace por ejecución?

Cuando las pruebas cambian configuración o despliegan varios componentes. Para una prueba pequeña puede bastar con etiquetas y nombres únicos, siempre que la limpieza pueda aislar exactamente sus recursos.

La idea central es simple: los datos de email de CI son recursos operativos, no basura anónima. Si tienen identidad, expiración y evidencia mínima, Kubernetes puede ayudar a limpiarlos sin borrar las señales que un equipo SRE necesita para entender el siguiente incidente.

global_articles.summary: This post walks through the Agents CLI evaluation loop for systematically improving agent performance through continuous testing and grading. global_articles.title: Three layers, one repo: a tour of google/adk-recipes
global_articles.summary: The google/adk-recipes repository unifies Agent Development Kit (ADK) resources into three structured layers—core/, plugins/, and contrib/—serving as a single source of truth for building AI agents. This cohesive structure streamlines the entire workflow from initial scaffolding to full deployment on Google Cloud infrastructure.

global_articles.title: Step by Step guide: Build a Voice Agent That Never Goes Silent using ADK
global_articles.summary: The open-source Agent Development Kit (ADK) and gemini-3.8-live enable developers to build responsive voice agents by implementing non-blocking tools in Python. Developers can use streaming tools to yield progress updates or background execution patterns to keep conversations fluid during long-running backend queries. Additionally, configuring response scheduling behaviors such as WHEN_IDLE, INTERRUPT, or SILENT gives developers precise control over when and how tool results are delivered into the conversation.

global_articles.title: Smaller apps and faster GPU inference with LiteRT in Google Play services
global_articles.summary: LiteRT in Google Play services now offers GPU inference powered by ML Drift, delivering about 1.4x faster performance alongside the new CompiledModel API. Switching from bundled binaries reduces app size by approximately 8 MB while enabling seamless, automatic runtime updates across billions of devices. Developers can easily adopt these updates by updating their dependencies and utilizing the new Android Studio LiteRT skill for automated migration.

global_articles.title: Unifying Edge AI: How Coral NPU’s open standard brings portable, energy-viable intelligence from model to silicon
global_articles.summary: Google Research has completed the 32-bit open-source Coral NPU RISC-V architecture with the introduction of its Matrix Execution Unit, which delivers up to 1 TOPS while targeting 10 mW average power for edge inference. Alongside this architecture, the release of the v1.0 open-source IREE/MLIR compiler allows developers to take models from JAX, PyTorch, and TensorFlow straight to Coral NPU hardware without writing custom assembly. global_articles.title: Fast, reliable A2UI, with swappable inference formats
global_articles.summary: A2UI now supports swappable inference formats, introducing A2UI Express which uses up to 3x fewer tokens and cuts latency by compiling compact Python-style syntax into standard A2UI JSON via Agent SDKs. global_articles.title: Build Generative UI Apps with A2UI & CopilotKit Agents

global_articles.title: Integrating TorchTPU into TorchTitan and Optimizing Models for TPU
global_articles.summary: TorchTPU integrates a native torch.device("tpu") backend directly into PyTorch, allowing developers to train large-scale models on Google Cloud TPUs without rewriting code in JAX. The TorchTitan TPU fork enhances this with production-grade scaling primitives like SimpleFSDP, Graph Trainer, and custom Pallas kernels that achieve high Model Flops Utilization (MFU) across dense and MoE architectures. Developers can leverage these battle-tested optimization playbooks, recipes, and the Hugging Face modeling backend to efficiently scale their own workloads on TPU infrastructure.

global_articles.title: Streaming comes to API Gateway: real-time and AI-ready APIs, without changing your spec
global_articles.summary: API Gateway now supports real-time streaming—including Server-Sent Events, WebSockets, gRPC, and chunked transfer encoding—in Public Preview without requiring changes to your existing API specifications.
